title: NASA Looking at Next Steps for Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
description: NASA is targeting early April for the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter to make the first attempt at powered, controlled flight of an aircraft on another planet. After Ingenuity is deployed from the rover, the 4-pound (1.8-kilogram) rotorcraft and the small team of engineers behind it will have 30 Martian days, or sols, (31 Earth days) to complete a series of flight tests. But the timeline leading up to the first flight and beyond depends on the helicopter meeting a series of daunting milestones first.   Ingenuity is currently attached to the belly of NASA’s Perseverance rover, which touched down on Mars Feb. 18, 2021. On Sunday, March 21, the rover deployed the debris shield that protected Ingenuity during landing, and is currently in transit to the first “airfield” on another planet where Ingenuity will attempt to fly.   For more information about Ingenuity, visit https://go.nasa.gov/ingenuity-press-kit and https://mars.nasa.gov/technology/helicopter.

and we've tested it in the simulated environment that we can create on Earth.
It really is time now to do the real flight test at Mars.

It's compared to Earth's density here in this room, you know, where at Mars is less than 1%, right?
So the first and foremost challenge is to make a vehicle that's light enough, you know, to be lifted.
And then second is to generate lift.
The rotor system has just been very fast.
Sometimes, you know, you have to do something just to show that you can do it,
in order to show that it's possible.
And so when the Wright brothers flew for the first time, you know, they didn't fly
fully equipped passenger airplane. They flew an experimental aircraft to show that it's possible
to do powered flights, sustained powered flight in Earth's atmosphere.
And in the same way, the Mars helicopter is designed to show that we can fly
powered helicopter flight in the Martian atmosphere.
It has to be fully autonomous from the time it takes off to the time it lands.
What we do do on the ground is we plan the flights and so we determine from here
where we want the helicopter to go in a particular flight.
Nothing is a given, but we have done everything we can in terms of a test program here in the
vehicles performing extremely well so far. It's been doing exactly the right thing even right now
when it's bolted on to the perseverance rover. So there's a very good chance that we'll pull it off,
yes, but it's still high risk. Most of the flights will be at the 3 to 5 meter height.

probably not much faster on these first flights. And then the 90 second flights means that you can
go about, you know, some couple of hundred meters or we'll probably go out 50, 70 meters and come back.
So it really depends on how much energy we have left over from our overnight and how comfortable we feel.
So I think in successive flights we'll probably push that further, try to go further.
